newsitem.title: GERMANY: Austria, German chancellors agree on Europe policy.
newsitem.headline: Austria, German chancellors agree on Europe policy.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl welcomed Austrian Chancellor Viktor Klima on Wednesday for talks on Europe's future that Bonn said took place in a "very friendly" atmosphere and showed broad agreement on policy.

Klima's one-day visit to Bonn -- his first trip abroad as chancellor -- was marked by discussions ranging from NATO expansion into eastern Europe to Austrian and German efforts to qualify for European economic and monetary union (EMU).

"Both chancellors determined there was broad agreement between German and Austrian positions in all questions regarding European policies," German government spokesman Peter Hausmann said in a statement.
Klima, a Social Democrat (SPOe), was Austrian finance minister until appointed chancellor in January after his predecessor Franz Vranitzky stepped down.
Talks with Kohl focused on preparation of the European Union's inter-governmental conference which will prepare for Europe's single currency launch in 1999, as well as EU and NATO expansion.

"They mutually stressed the goal that the European Council meeting in Amsterdam in June should be concluded with a result that promotes the continuation of the process of European integration," Hausmann added.
Before meeting Kohl, Klima met German President Roman Herzog over breakfast and then took a tour of Bonn's Art and Exhibition Hall to see an exhibition of paintings.
He also met Finance Minister Theo Waigel and the two reaffirmed their countries' determination to qualify for EMU.

Waigel, under pressure to whip Germany's state finances into shape to meet the Maastricht treaty goals for EMU, said the timetable for monetary union was not as important as fulfilling the fiscal goals.
Yet a German government spokesman later denied that Chancellor Kohl was seeking a delay in the launch of EMU and dispelled rumours that Kohl was about to resign over the issue.

Germany, among the most outspoken advocates of a strict interpretation of the treaty, itself runs a high risk of failing the budget deficit yardsticks this year, by which European Union members will be assessed for EMU.

Germany must fight rising unemployment and boost growth to meet the targets, Waigel said, adding: "If we are successful in getting unemployment down by the beginning of the summer we can fulfil the criteria."

Klima took a less strict view and said it was more important that a country's finances demonstrated clearly that it was moving in the right direction, particularly in respect of the Maastricht debt criterion.
He said he was opposed to renegotiating the Maastricht treaty, but added "We should use the room available in the treaty to interpret the criteria."
The European Union members who will participate in the first wave of EMU in 1999 will be chosen early next year based on their fiscal performance in 1997.
Participants must meet a number of financial criteria including restricting budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product and total public debt to 60 percent.
Klima ended his visit with talks with German Social Democrat (SPD) leader Oskar Lafontaine, which he said focused on tackling soaring unemployment in Europe.

Klima said the EU should add a section on employment to the Maastricht treaty. "European Union Labour Ministers must fight unemployment with the same commitment as Finance Ministers fight for budget and currency stability," Klima said.
